# What happens in a round?

*This chapter is a tour. It uses every term the rest of the guide defines, loosely, so you have the map before the
detail. Don't stop on a word you don't know: its chapter is named next to it.*

## The story

On 3 November we ran a rehearsal of round 1 against an exchange we had never seen, the Varde Exchange. It was built to
be unlike anything the repo knew: its own data layout, its own way of calling the bot, prices in cents on a five-cent
step, results in euros, and a scoring program written separately from our engine. A fresh agent session got the same
prompt it will get on the day and a one-hour clock. Here is what it did [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/DRYRUN_LOG.md`)]{.src}.

- **0:00.** It read the rules: three products, LUMEN, QUILL and SORREL, each with a *position limit* (40, 60 and 30
  lots: how much of it you may hold, long or short). Orders *rest* until filled or cancelled. A fee is charged per lot
  traded *and* per order placed. Three public sessions of data; the score comes from two hidden ones.
- **0:03.** It wrote a *format plug-in*, the piece of code that reads this exchange's files into the engine's own
  shape (chapter 9), and ran `arena.diagnose`, which describes each product from the data alone: does its price wander
  or come back to a level, how wide is its *spread*, how often does it jump (chapter 3).
- **0:05.** It wrote the bot: the repo's *template*, with settings for each product, and the *adapter* that speaks
  this exchange's language. Its first *backtest*, a replay of the public sessions with the bot trading in them, made
  730 euros.
- **0:06.** A *grid*: every combination of a few settings, each backtested, under two *fill models* (chapter 6). One
  product, SORREL, did better taking only, never quoting.
- **0:07.** `arena.validate` checked the file against the rules (size, speed, no outside libraries), and it was
  uploaded. The portal scored it **€367.61** on the public sessions and returned twelve figures and a file of every
  fill.
- **0:09.** It ran *calibrate*, which searches our engine's settings for one that reproduces the portal's twelve
  figures (chapter 8). Calibrate **refused**: no setting came within 5%, the closest was 98% off. The session did what
  the refusal says. It didn't paste a setting into the engine; it rebuilt the score by hand from the fills file and
  found why. The fee per order placed was 28% of what the bot made before fees, and the exchange filled resting orders
  from only half of each trade, which our engine didn't know.
- **0:14.** It stopped, as told, after one validated upload and an honest reading of it.

On the hidden sessions the bot scored **€208.77**, against **€80.10** for the example bot the exchange handed out
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/README.md`)]{.src}.

## The idea

A round is a loop (@fig-loop), run as many times as five hours and the submission limit allow.

![The round's loop. The first lap should end in a validated upload by two hours in (`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round").](figures/f01_round_loop.png){#fig-loop
fig-alt="A loop of eight boxes: the round's data and rules, diagnose, the bot, backtest and grid, validate, upload, the portal's figures, calibrate, and back to the start."}

1. **Read the market.** The data is a recording: the *order book* at every *tick* (who is offering to buy and sell,
   at what prices, how much) and the trades that happened. Chapter 2 is the order book; chapter 3 is the price.
2. **Write the bot.** A bot is called once a tick, sees the book and its own position, and returns orders. Ours is
   mostly a *market maker*: it offers to buy a little below the fair price and to sell a little above it, and earns
   the gap, the spread, when others trade with it. Chapter 4 says why that pays at all; chapter 5 says who it loses to.
3. **Backtest.** Replay the recorded days with the bot in them. The replay has to guess what would have happened to
   orders that weren't really there, and the guess, the fill model, can be worth more than the strategy. Chapter 6.
4. **Choose settings without fooling yourself.** A grid tries many settings; the best of many is flattered by luck,
   and three days of data are very few. Chapter 7.
5. **Upload, and read what comes back.** The portal is the only judge that matters. Its figures say how far our replay
   is from the real exchange, and calibrate turns that into engine settings, or refuses. Chapter 8.

Two habits make the loop work. **Upload early**: the first validated upload by two hours in, so there is always
something scored. **Change one thing at a time**, and only what the evidence supports, because each upload is one
noisy measurement and submissions are limited.

## What this rehearsal teaches

The rehearsal's most useful moment was the refusal. A tool that always gives an answer would have handed over the
least-bad setting, 98% off, and the next five hours of backtests would have been tuned to an engine that wasn't the
exchange's. A tool that says "no setting fits, here are the likely causes" sent the session to the one place the truth
was, the portal's own fills. Most of this guide is about that distinction: what our tools can measure, what they can
only assume, and how to tell the two apart under time pressure.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
The loop is model development against a black-box evaluator: a local validation set (the backtest), a hidden test
set (the scored sessions), and a limited number of test-set queries (the uploads). The analogy holds well, with two
breaks. The local validator is a simulator with a known bias, not a held-out sample of the same data (chapter 6). And
every query to the test set costs one of a handful of submissions, so each is planned like an experiment.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="In the repo"}

- The loop's tools: `arena.diagnose`, `arena.backtest`, `arena.grid`, `arena.validate`, `experiments.day.calibrate`.
- The kickoff prompt the session got: `KICKOFF_PROMPT.md`, round 1.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="On the day"}
`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round", is this loop with times on it. `KICKOFF_PROMPT.md` starts the session that runs it.
:::
